a1-greetings.title: Greetings: Hala and Marhaba
a1-greetings.explanation: Emirati Arabic has several everyday greetings. "هلا" (hala) and "مرحبا" (marhaba) are casual hellos used constantly in daily life. "السلام عليكم" (as-salaamu alaykum, "peace be upon you") is the more formal/traditional Islamic greeting, answered with "وعليكم السلام" (wa alaykum as-salaam). "شلونك؟" (shlonak?) asks "how are you?" and is typically answered "زين، الحمد لله" (zayn, alhamdulillah — "good, thank God").
a1-greetings.fact: Emirati greetings often stack: a full exchange might go "السلام عليكم" → "وعليكم السلام" → "شلونك؟" → "زين، الحمد لله. وانت؟" — layering several greeting formulas together is completely normal and expected, not redundant.

dialogue.en: Peace be upon you! How are you today?

dialogue.native: وعليكم السلام. زين، الحمد لله. وانت؟
dialogue.en: And peace be upon you. Good, thank God. And you?

a1-present-shirib.title: Present Tense: I Drink, You Drink...
a1-present-shirib.explanation: Emirati present-tense verbs take a prefix (and sometimes a suffix) that shows who's doing the action: أشرب (ashrab, "I drink"), تشرب (tishrab, "you-m drink"), تشربي (tishrabi, "you-f drink"), يشرب (yishrab, "he drinks"), تشرب (tishrab, "she drinks", same as you-m), نشرب (nishrab, "we drink"), تشربون (tishrabuun, "you-all drink"), يشربون (yishrabuun, "they drink").
a1-present-shirib.fact: Notice "you-m drink" (تشرب tishrab) and "she drinks" (تشرب tishrab) look identical in writing and sound — context (who's being talked about) is what tells them apart, exactly the way English "read" sounds the same in present tense regardless of subject.

dialogue.en: I'm drinking coffee now and tea later

a1-negation.title: Negation: Ma and Mub
a1-negation.explanation: To say a verb didn't/doesn't happen, put ما (ma) right before it: ما أبغى (ma abgha, "I don't want"). To negate a nominal sentence (no verb, just "X is Y"), Emirati uses مب (mub) instead: أنا مب تعبان (ana mub ta3baan, "I'm not tired").
a1-negation.fact: Getting ما and مب mixed up is one of the most common learner mistakes — remember the split by what follows: ما goes with an action (a verb), مب goes with a description (an adjective or noun after a pronoun).

dialogue.native: لا، أنا مب تعبان، أنا مبسوط
dialogue.en: No, I'm not tired, I'm happy

a2-past-raah.title: Past Tense: I Went, You Went...
a2-past-raah.pattern: رحت / رحت / رحتي / راح / راحت / رحنا / رحتو / راحو
a2-past-raah.explanation: The past tense of راح (raah, "to go") is formed with suffixes attached to the root ر-و-ح: رحت (riHt, "I went"), رحت (riHt, "you-m went"), رحتي (riHti, "you-f went"), راح (raah, "he went"), راحت (raaHat, "she went"), رحنا (riHna, "we went"), رحتو (riHtaw, "you-all went"), راحو (raaHaw, "they went").
a2-past-raah.fact: Notice the vowel shift: the medial "aa" of راح shortens to a plain "i" in every person except he/she/they (راح/راحت/راحو keep the long "aa"). This a→i shift in all-but-third-person is a very common pattern across Gulf Arabic past-tense verbs, not unique to راح.

dialogue.en: I went home, and I saw the family, good

a2-past-shaaf.title: Past Tense: I Saw, You Saw...
a2-past-shaaf.pattern: شفت / شفت / شفتي / شاف / شافت / شفنا / شفتو / شافو
a2-past-shaaf.explanation: The past tense of شاف (shaaf, "to see") follows the same pattern as راح: شفت (shift, "I saw"), شفت (shift, "you-m saw"), شفتي (shifti, "you-f saw"), شاف (shaaf, "he saw"), شافت (shaafat, "she saw"), شفنا (shifna, "we saw"), شفتو (shiftaw, "you-all saw"), شافو (shaafaw, "they saw").
a2-past-shaaf.fact: Many Emirati speakers pronounce this verb with چ instead of ش (چاف/چفت, chaaf/chift) — a well-known regional sound shift found in parts of the UAE and wider Gulf, and both pronunciations are considered correct.

dialogue.en: Did you (f) see the family yesterday?

dialogue.native: نعم، شفت الأهل، وشفت صديق زين
dialogue.en: Yes, I saw the family, and I saw a good friend

a2-past-negation.title: Negating the Past: Ma + Past Verb
a2-past-negation.explanation: To negate a past-tense verb, put ما (ma) right before it, exactly like with the present tense: ما رحت (ma riHt, "I didn't go"), ما شفت (ma shift, "I didn't see").
a2-past-negation.fact: Unlike the present tense (which splits between ما for verbs and مب for nominal sentences), the past tense always uses ما — there's no مب-equivalent for past-tense negation, which simplifies this pattern compared to the present.

dialogue.en: Did you see the family yesterday?

dialogue.native: لا، ما شفت الأهل، رحت الحين بس
dialogue.en: No, I didn't see the family, I only went now

a2-days-past.title: Days of the Week with Past Tense
a2-days-past.explanation: Combining a day name with a past-tense verb is a natural way to build a simple narrative: يوم الجمعة رحت البيت (yoom el-jum3a riHt el-bayt, "On Friday I went home"). The day name simply comes first, exactly like a time adverb.
a2-days-past.fact: Notice there's no extra preposition needed before the day name ("on Friday") — Emirati, like most Gulf dialects, places time expressions directly at the start of the sentence without a linking word.

dialogue.en: On Saturday, where did you go?

dialogue.native: يوم السبت رحت البيت وشفت الأهل
dialogue.en: On Saturday I went home and saw the family

b1-3ind.title: Possession: Aandi, Aandak, Aandah...
b1-3ind.pattern: عندي / عندك / عنده / عندها / عندنا / عندكم / عندهم
b1-3ind.explanation: Arabic has no verb "to have" — instead, Emirati uses عند (aand, literally "at/by") fused with a person ending: عندي (aandi, "I have"), عندك (aandak, "you-m have"), عنده (aandah, "he has"), عندها (aandaha, "she has"), عندنا (aandana, "we have"), عندكم (aandakum, "you-all have"), عندهم (aandahum, "they have"). Negate it with ما: ما عندي (ma aandi, "I don't have").
b1-3ind.fact: عند expresses lasting/permanent possession (owning something), which is different from مع (ma3a, "with") used for what someone is physically carrying right now — a distinction English doesn't make with a single word "have."

dialogue.en: Yes, I have money, thank God

b1-lian.title: Because: Lian
b1-lian.explanation: لأن (li-ann, "because") introduces a reason: أنا تعبان لأن رحت البيت أمس (ana ta3baan li-ann riHt el-bayt ams, "I'm tired because I went home yesterday"). It always comes right before the reason clause, same position as English "because."
b1-lian.fact: لأن can also open a sentence to answer a "why" question directly: ليش انت تعبان؟ لأن ما شربت قهوة (leish inta ta3baan? li-ann ma shirabt gahwa — "Why are you tired? Because I didn't drink coffee").

dialogue.en: Why do you have a lot of money?

dialogue.native: لأن أشرب قهوة بس، ما أبغى شي غالي
dialogue.en: Because I only drink coffee, I don't want anything expensive
